Effect of nonlinear diffusion on a lower bound
for the blow-up time
in a fully parabolic chemotaxis system

Teruto Nishino00 0 E-mail addresses: teruto.nishino@gmail.com, yokota@rs.kagu.tus.ac.jp

Tomomi Yokota** * Corresponding author.†† † Partially supported by Grant-in-Aid for Scientific Research (C), No. 25400119.

Department of Mathematics

Tokyo University of Science

August 24, 2026

  • Abstract. This paper deals with a lower bound for the blow-up time for solutions of the fully parabolic chemotaxis system

    {ut=∇⋅[(u+α)m1−1∇u−χu(u+α)m2−2∇v]in​Ω×(0,T),vt=Δ​v−v+uin​Ω×(0,T)\begin{cases}u_{t}=\nabla\cdot[(u+\alpha)^{m_{1}-1}\nabla u-\chi u(u+\alpha)^{m_{2}-2}\nabla v]&{\rm in}\;\Omega\times(0,T),\\[2.84526pt] v_{t}=\Delta v-v+u&{\rm in}\;\Omega\times(0,T)\\[2.84526pt] \end{cases}

    under Neumann boundary conditions and initial conditions, where Ω\Omega is a general bounded domain in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} with smooth boundary, α>0\alpha>0, χ>0\chi>0, m1,m2∈ℝm_{1},m_{2}\in\mathbb{R} and T>0T>0. Recently, Anderson–Deng [1] gave a lower bound for the blow-up time in the case that m1=1m_{1}=1 and Ω\Omega is a convex bounded domain. The purpose of this paper is to generalize the result in [1] to the case that m1≠1m_{1}\neq 1 and Ω\Omega is a non-convex bounded domain. The key to the proof is to make a sharp estimate by using the Gagliardo–Nirenberg inequality and an inequality for boundary integrals. As a consequence, the main result of this paper reflects the effect of nonlinear diffusion and need not assume the convexity of Ω\Omega.

1 Introduction

In this paper we consider a lower bound for the blow-up time in the following fully parabolic chemotaxis system with nonlinear diffusion:

(1.1) {ut=∇⋅[(u+α)m1−1∇u−χu(u+α)m2−2∇v]in​Ω×(0,T),vt=Δ​v−v+uin​Ω×(0,T),∇u⋅ν=∇v⋅ν=0on​∂Ω×(0,T),u⁡(⋅,0)=u0,v⁡(⋅,0)=v0in​Ω,\begin{cases}u_{t}=\nabla\cdot[(u+\alpha)^{m_{1}-1}\nabla u-\chi u(u+\alpha)^{m_{2}-2}\nabla v]&{\rm in}\ \Omega\times(0,T),\\[2.84526pt] v_{t}=\Delta v-v+u&{\rm in}\ \Omega\times(0,T),\\[5.69054pt] \nabla u\cdot\nu=\nabla v\cdot\nu=0&{\rm on}\ \partial\Omega\times(0,T),\\[2.84526pt] u(\cdot,0)=u_{0},\ v(\cdot,0)=v_{0}&{\rm in}\ \Omega,\end{cases}

where Ω\Omega is a general bounded domain in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} (n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}) with smooth boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega and ν\nu is the outward normal vector to ∂Ω\partial\Omega and T>0T>0. The initial data u0u_{0} and v0v_{0} are supposed to be nonnegative functions such that u0∈C⁡(Ω¯)u_{0}\in C(\overline{\Omega}) and v0∈C1​(Ω¯)v_{0}\in C^{1}(\overline{\Omega}). Also we assume that

α>0,χ>0,m1,m2∈ℝ.\displaystyle\alpha>0,\quad\chi>0,\quad m_{1},m_{2}\in\mathbb{R}.

In the system (1.1), the unknown function u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) represents the density of the cell population and the unknown function v⁡(x,t)v(x,t) shows the concentration of the signal substance at place xx and time tt. The system (1.1) with the simplest choices m1=1m_{1}=1 and m2=2m_{2}=2 describes a part of life cycle of cellular slime molds with chemotaxis and it was proposed by Keller–Segel [18] in 1970. After that, a quasilinear system such as (1.1) was proposed by Painter–Hillen [25]. A number of variations of the original Keller–Segel system are proposed and investigated (see e.g., Bellomo–Bellouquid–Tao–Winkler [2], Hillen–Painter [9] and Horstmann [10, 11]).

According to a continuity model, the first equation in (1.1) has the flux vector F=−[(u+α)m1−1∇u−χu(u+α)m2−2∇v]F=-\left[(u+\alpha)^{m_{1}-1}\nabla u-\chi u(u+\alpha)^{m_{2}-2}\nabla v\right]. We can recognize that (u+α)m1−1∇u(u+\alpha)^{m_{1}-1}\nabla u represents the diffusive flux and −χu(u+α)m2−2∇v-\chi u(u+\alpha)^{m_{2}-2}\nabla v represents the chemotactic flux modelling undirected cell migration and the advective flux with velocity dependent on the gradient of the signal. More precisely, when cellular slime molds plunge into hunger, they move towards higher concentrations of the chemical substance secreted by cells.

From a mathematical point of view, uu in (1.1) enjoys the mass conservation property:

∫Ωu⁡(⋅,t)=∫Ωu0\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}u(\cdot,t)=\int_{\Omega}u_{0}

for all t∈(0,T)t\in(0,T). It is a meaningful question whether solutions of (1.1) remain bounded or blow up. As to this question, it is known that the borderline between boundedness and blow-up is the case that m2=m1+2nm_{2}=m_{1}+\frac{2}{n}, m1≥1m_{1}\geq 1, m2≥2m_{2}\geq 2. According to the result established by Horstmann–Winkler [12, Theorems 4.1 and 6.1] in the case m1=1m_{1}=1, it can be expected that (1.1) has a global bounded solution in the case that m2<m1+2nm_{2}<m_{1}+\frac{2}{n} and a blow-up solution in the case that m2>m1+2nm_{2}>m_{1}+\frac{2}{n}. Indeed, in the case that Ω\Omega is a bounded domain and m2<m1+2nm_{2}<m_{1}+\frac{2}{n}, there exists a global bounded solution of (1.1) (see Tao–Winkler [33], Ishida–Seki–Yokota [13] and Senba–Suzuki [31]). In addition, this result was shown also for the degenerate chemotaxis system ((1.1) with α=0\alpha=0) (see Ishida–Yokota [14, 16] when Ω=ℝn\Omega=\mathbb{R}^{n} and m2<m1+2nm_{2}<m_{1}+\frac{2}{n}; [13] when Ω\Omega is a bounded domain and m2<m1+2nm_{2}<m_{1}+\frac{2}{n}; Mimura [23] when Ω\Omega is a bounded domain with Dirichlet–Neumann boundary condition, m2=2m_{2}=2 and m1>2−2nm_{1}>2-\frac{2}{n}). If m2≥m1+2nm_{2}\geq m_{1}+\frac{2}{n}, then the results are divided by the size of initial data. For example, the system (1.1) has a global solution with small initial data when Ω=ℝn\Omega=\mathbb{R}^{n} and α=0\alpha=0 even if m2≥m1+2nm_{2}\geq m_{1}+\frac{2}{n} (see Ishida–Yokota [15]). On the other hand, in the case that Ω=BR:={x∈ℝn||x|<R}\Omega=B_{R}:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\big||x|<R\} (R>0)(R>0), m1=1m_{1}=1, m2=2m_{2}=2, n≥3n\geq 3, which implies m2>m1+2nm_{2}>m_{1}+\frac{2}{n}, there exist initial data such that the radially symmetric solution of (1.1) blows up in finite time (see Winkler [34]). The result was extended to the case that Ω=BR\Omega=B_{R}, m2>m1+2nm_{2}>m_{1}+\frac{2}{n}, n≥2n\geq 2 (see Cieślak–Stinner [3, 4] when α>0\alpha>0, Hashira–Ishida–Yokota [8] when α=0\alpha=0). In the most important case that Ω=BR\Omega=B_{R}, m1=1m_{1}=1, m2=2m_{2}=2, n=2n=2, which implies m2=m1+2nm_{2}=m_{1}+\frac{2}{n}, there exist initial data such that the corresponding solutions of (1.1) blow up in finite time (see Mizoguchi–Winkler [24]).

We are especially interested in a lower bound for the blow-up time for solutions of (1.1), because it seems to be important to know how m1m_{1} affects on the blow-up time for solutions of (1.1). The study of a lower bound for the blow-up time seems to be interesting widely for general parabolic systems (see Payne–Schaefer [27] and Enache [5]), wave equations (see Philippin [30]) and heat equations (see Payne–Philippin–Vernier Piro [26]). Moreover, explicit lower bounds for the blow-up time for solutions of various semilinear parabolic equations were obtained by [27]. As to chemotaxis systems, Payne–Song [28, 29] established a lower bound of blow-up time for solutions of (1.1) with m1=1m_{1}=1 and m2=2m_{2}=2 in the form

t~∗≥∫Φ1​(0)∞d​ξV​ξ32+W​ξ2(n=2)\displaystyle\widetilde{t}^{\ast}\geq\int_{\Phi_{1}(0)}^{\infty}\frac{d\xi}{V{\xi}^{\frac{3}{2}}+W{\xi}^{2}}\quad(n=2)

and

t~∗≥∫Φ1​(0)∞d​ξX​ξ32+Y​ξ3(n=3);\displaystyle\widetilde{t}^{\ast}\geq\int_{\Phi_{1}(0)}^{\infty}\frac{d\xi}{X{\xi}^{\frac{3}{2}}+Y{\xi}^{3}}\quad(n=3);

note that t~∗\widetilde{t}^{\ast} means the blow-up time in Φ1\Phi_{1}-measure, i.e., limt↗t~∗Φ1​(t)=∞\lim_{t\nearrow\widetilde{t}^{\ast}}\Phi_{1}(t)=\infty, where Φ1​(t)\Phi_{1}(t) is defined as

(1.2) Φ1​(t):=κ​∫Ωu​(⋅,t)2+∫Ω|Δ​v​(⋅,t)|2(t>0)\displaystyle\Phi_{1}(t):=\kappa\int_{\Omega}{u(\cdot,t)}^{2}+\int_{\Omega}|\Delta v(\cdot,t)|^{2}\quad(t>0)

with some κ>0\kappa>0. When Ω\Omega is a convex bounded domain and m1=1m_{1}=1, Li–Zheng [19] gave a lower bound for the blow-up time for solutions of (1.1) by using (1.2) in the case that m2∈(53,2]m_{2}\in(\frac{5}{3},2], n=3n=3 and in the case that m2∈[2,3)m_{2}\in[2,3), n=2n=2. After that, when Ω=B1\Omega=B_{1}, α=1\alpha=1 and m1=1m_{1}=1, in the case that m2∈[53,3]m_{2}\in[\frac{5}{3},3] and n=3n=3, Tao–Vernier Piro [32] introduced the measure Φ2​(t)\Phi_{2}(t) in the form

(1.3) Φ2​(t):=∫Ω(u⁡(⋅,t)+1)p+∫Ω|∇v​(⋅,t)|2​q(t>0)\displaystyle\Phi_{2}(t):=\int_{\Omega}\left(u(\cdot,t)+1\right)^{p}+\int_{\Omega}\left|\nabla v(\cdot,t)\right|^{2q}\quad(t>0)

for suitable p,q>1p,q>1 (p=2p=2 and q=4q=4 when m2∈[53,2]m_{2}\in[\frac{5}{3},2]; p=5p=5 and q=22q=22 when m2∈(2,3]m_{2}\in(2,3]) from the view point of local existence of classical solutions to (1.1) and an initial datum v0∈W1,q​(Ω)v_{0}\in W^{1,q}(\Omega) (see [2, Lemma 3.1]). This restriction on m2m_{2} and nn was removed by Anderson–Deng [1] when Ω\Omega is a convex bounded domain and m1=1m_{1}=1. Furthermore, as a new attempt to estimating a lower bound for the blow-up time in the above sense, Marras–Vernier Piro–Viglialoro [21, 22] obtained a lower bound for the blow-up time of the more generalized equation with a source term:

(1.4) {ut=∇⋅[∇u−k1(t)um2−1∇v]+f(u)in​Ω×(0,T),vt=k2​(t)​Δ​v−k3​(t)​v+k4​(t)​uin​Ω×(0,T)\begin{cases}u_{t}=\nabla\cdot[\nabla u-k_{1}(t)u^{m_{2}-1}\nabla v]+{\boldmath f(u)}&{\rm in}\;\Omega\times(0,T),\\[2.84526pt] v_{t}=k_{2}(t)\Delta v-k_{3}(t)v+k_{4}(t)u&{\rm in}\;\Omega\times(0,T)\\[2.84526pt] \end{cases}

under Neumann boundary conditions and initial conditions, where ki​(t)​(i=1,2,3,4)k_{i}(t)\ (i=1,2,3,4) are nonnegative smooth functions of tt, m2∈[2,3)m_{2}\in[2,3) when n=2n=2, m2∈(53,2)m_{2}\in(\frac{5}{3},2) when n=3n=3, ff satisfies f⁡(u)≤c​u2f(u)\leq cu^{2} with c>0c>0. A similar result for the parabolic–elliptic version of (1.4) was deduced by Jiao–Zeng [17].

Now we focus on the studies obtained by [32] and [1] which gave a lower bound for the blow-up time for solutions of (1.1) under the following conditions:

  • •

    “m1=1m_{1}=1”, m2∈[53,3]m_{2}\in[\frac{5}{3},3], n=3n=3, Ω\Omega is a unit ball B1⊂ℝ3B_{1}\subset\boldmath\mathbb{R}^{3} ([32]);

  • •

    “m1=1m_{1}=1”, m2∈ℝm_{2}\in\mathbb{R}, n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, Ω\Omega is a convex bounded domain in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} ([1]).

However, there is still room for improvements in these results. More precisely, we cannot find any results in the nonlinear case that m1≠1m_{1}\neq 1 and Ω\Omega is a non-convex bounded domain. Hence the current situation is summarized in Table 1.
